sections.p01.s0: Seven small programs, one per day, each built around one language feature. Spend the first hour on the feature in the tutorial, the rest writing the program from a blank file. Commit each day's program to Git; Day 7 has no tutorial open at all.
sections.p01.s1: The standard-library modules every real script uses. Study one module per day (s1.0 to s1.5) with a short script for each, then spend the last two days on the File Organizer, which uses all of them together.
sections.p01.s2: Automated testing with pytest. Learn the tool (s2.0 to s2.3) in the first half of the week on small examples, then spend the second half retrofitting tests onto your own projects and proving they catch bugs.
sections.p01.s3: Classes and the data model. Take the concepts in order (s3.0 to s3.4), about a day each with small examples, then build the Inventory Engine with tests and refactor it once it works.
sections.p01.s4: A checklist applied to every project from here on, not a week of work. Check each project against all five items before you call it finished, and fix any that fail.

p01.s0.0.how: Write one function per operation and a loop that reads 'number operator number'. Catch ValueError for bad numbers and ZeroDivisionError separately. Keep past results in a list and add a history command.
p01.s0.0.done: Typing 'abc', '5 / 0' and 'history' each gives a clear message and the program keeps running.

p01.s0.1.how: Use random.randint for the secret number and if/elif/else for too high, too low and correct. Difficulty sets the range and attempt limit; score depends on attempts left; ask to replay at the end.
p01.s0.1.done: You can play three rounds on different difficulties without restarting, and invalid guesses do not crash it.

p01.s0.2.how: Build the character pool from string.ascii_letters, digits and punctuation as chosen, and pick with secrets.choice in a loop. Score strength from length and the number of character classes used.
p01.s0.2.done: You can explain why secrets and not random is used for passwords.

p01.s0.3.how: Read a text file, split words with str.split after lower-casing and stripping punctuation, split sentences on full stops, question marks and exclamation marks, and count words with collections.Counter. Print the top 10 and the average word and sentence length.
p01.s0.3.done: Word counts on a short paragraph match a count you did by hand.

p01.s0.4.how: Store each task as a tuple (title, done) in a list, and replace the tuple to mark it complete, since tuples are immutable. Implement add, remove by number, complete and list as commands in a loop.
p01.s0.4.done: You can explain why marking a task complete replaces the tuple instead of changing it.

p01.s0.5.how: Store contacts in a dict keyed by name, each with a phone, an email and a set of tags. Search by partial name, and find contacts sharing tags with set intersection (&).
p01.s0.5.done: Adding a duplicate tag has no effect, and a tag search returns exactly the contacts you expect.

p01.s0.6.how: Choose a small app you have not built (unit converter, quiz, expense log). Write the requirements in five lines first, then build it with only the Python docs open.
p01.s0.6.done: The app meets all five written requirements and no tutorial was open while you built it.

p01.s1.0.how: Split a script into two modules and import one from the other. Print __name__ in both, add an if __name__ == "__main__": block, and print sys.path to see where imports are searched.
p01.s1.0.done: You can say what __name__ is when a file is run directly and when it is imported.

p01.s1.1.how: Define class ValidationError(Exception), raise it with a message from a validation function, and catch only that type at the call site. Use raise ... from err when re-raising.
p01.s1.1.done: You can explain why except Exception around a whole function hides bugs.

p01.s1.2.how: Rewrite a script that uses string paths with Path: build paths with /, list files with iterdir and glob, read with read_text, and create folders with mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True).
p01.s1.2.done: The script has no os.path.join or string concatenation for paths and runs on your machine.

p01.s1.3.how: Save your contact manager to JSON with json.dump and load it back; convert sets to lists first. Export the same data with csv.DictWriter, opening the file with newline="", and read it back.
p01.s1.3.done: Saving and reloading gives data equal to the original, checked with ==.

p01.s1.4.how: Work through the argparse HOWTO, then give one of your programs positional arguments, a --dry-run flag with action="store_true", and typed options. Run it with --help.
p01.s1.4.done: --help prints usage for every option and bad arguments give an error, not a traceback.

p01.s1.5.how: Replace the prints in a script with logger = logging.getLogger(__name__) calls at the right levels. Configure basicConfig once in main to write to a file with timestamps, and log errors with logger.exception.
p01.s1.5.done: The log file shows timestamp, level and message for each run, including a traceback for a forced error.

p01.s1.6.how: Order: plan moves by extension, apply them with shutil.move and record each in a JSON journal, add --dry-run to print the plan only, --undo to replay the journal backwards, and SHA-256 hashing for duplicates.
p01.s1.6.done: On a test folder, organise then undo returns every file to its original path, and dry-run changes nothing.

p01.s2.0.how: Install with uv add --dev pytest. Write test_*.py files with test_* functions using plain assert, run uv run pytest -q, then try -k to select tests and -x to stop at the first failure.
p01.s2.0.done: You can say which files and functions pytest collects and read a failing assertion's output.

p01.s2.1.how: Rewrite three tests so each has three blocks separated by blank lines: arrange the inputs, act with one call, assert on the result. Split any test that checks two behaviours into two tests.
p01.s2.1.done: Each test name describes one behaviour, and when a test fails the name tells you what broke.

p01.s2.2.how: For one function, list inputs for each category and turn them into pytest.mark.parametrize cases. Use pytest.raises for expected errors, and monkeypatch to raise PermissionError, since Windows file permissions are hard to fake.
p01.s2.2.done: Your tests cover all five categories and each one passes or led to a fix.

p01.s2.3.how: Write a fixture that builds a small folder tree inside tmp_path, then use it in tests of your file code. Never touch real folders in tests; tmp_path gives each test its own new directory.
p01.s2.3.done: Your filesystem tests pass in any order and leave nothing behind in your project folder.

p01.s2.4.how: Start with the pure functions (calculator operations, move planning), then the file-touching parts using tmp_path, then dry-run and undo. Commit after each group passes.
p01.s2.4.done: Both projects have a test suite that passes with pytest, including a dry-run test and an undo test.

p01.s2.5.how: Introduce one bug at a time (off-by-one, wrong comparison operator, a swallowed exception), run the suite, then git restore the file. Write a new test for any bug that got through.
p01.s2.5.done: Each of the three bugs makes at least one test fail, and the suite passes again after restoring.

p01.s3.0.how: Write a small class with a class attribute and instance attributes set in __init__. Inspect vars(obj) and type(obj).__dict__, then shadow the class attribute on one instance and see which value each instance reads.
p01.s3.0.done: You can say the lookup order: instance, then class, then base classes.

p01.s3.1.how: Model a Warehouse twice: once inheriting from list, once holding a list as an attribute. Note which list methods the first version exposes that a warehouse should not have.
p01.s3.1.done: For any two of your classes you can say whether the relation is is-a or has-a, and justify it.

p01.s3.2.how: Add a @property with a setter that rejects negative prices, a @classmethod from_dict as an alternative constructor, and a @staticmethod helper that uses neither the class nor an instance.
p01.s3.2.done: Setting a negative price raises ValueError, and you can say when to use each of the three decorators.

p01.s3.3.how: Rewrite a plain class as @dataclass and compare the generated __repr__ and __eq__. Try frozen=True, and use field(default_factory=list) for a mutable default.
p01.s3.3.done: You can explain why a mutable default like items: list = [] is rejected by dataclasses.

p01.s3.4.how: Give a Category class __repr__, __eq__ that returns NotImplemented for other types, __len__ and __iter__. Then test len(), ==, a for loop, and whether instances still work in a set.
p01.s3.4.done: You can explain why defining __eq__ alone makes instances unhashable.

p01.s3.5.how: Order: Product and Category as dataclasses, Warehouse holding stock counts, Customer, then Order with lines that reserves stock and fails cleanly when stock runs out. Write tests for each class as you go.
p01.s3.5.done: Tests pass for placing an order, rejecting one that exceeds stock, and stock totals after both.

p01.s3.6.how: With the tests passing, list the three worst parts (long methods, duplicated logic, unclear names) and fix one at a time, running the tests and committing after each change.
p01.s3.6.done: The tests pass unchanged after the refactor, and git log shows separate commits for each change.

p01.s4.0.how: Search each project for except: and pass inside except blocks. Replace each with the specific exception type and a real action: log it, re-raise it, or return an error value.
p01.s4.0.done: No search hits remain, and every except block names an exception type and does something with it.

p01.s4.1.how: Move paths, limits and other settings into a config.toml read once with tomllib at startup, or into environment variables via os.environ. Pass the values into functions as arguments.
p01.s4.1.done: You can change a setting without editing any file that contains business logic.

p01.s4.2.how: Log the start and end of each operation with its inputs and IDs, log decisions at INFO, and use logger.exception in except blocks. Then break an input and diagnose it from the log alone.
p01.s4.2.done: Someone reading only the log file can say what the program was doing when it failed and with which input.

p01.s4.3.how: Write four headed sections: install (exact commands), usage (example commands and output), design decisions (why, not what), and limitations (what it does not handle). Follow the install steps in a fresh clone.
p01.s4.3.done: A fresh clone installs and runs using only the README's commands.

p01.s4.4.how: Commit after each working change. Write the subject in the imperative, under about 50 characters ('Add undo to organiser'), and a body for the why when it is not obvious. Stage related changes together with git add -p.

where.name: How to write a Git commit message
Pro Git: Contributing to a project

p01.s4.4.done: Reading git log --oneline alone tells you how the project was built, step by step.
